title: Floating over the beat unlike Eddie Lang
summary: Rosenberg says his playing stood out for floating away from the beat and returning, unlike Eddie Lang; Bunn says that is how his mind went.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Very driving. I was wondering, Teddy,

this is maybe a kind of crazy question, but bear with me, you know? I was wondering like, when you -- a couple of things. One is that one of the things that I feel made your guitar playing distinctive for that early, you know --
What do you mean, now?
Well, one of the things that made your playing special.
Yeah.
Particularly in the '30s.
Yeah.
Was the way you would get away from the beat. You know, they'd be holding the beat down.
Yeah.
But you would play -- you would sort of float over it.
Oh, I had to.
Got away from it. Well, a lot of guitarists, for example, Eddy Lang, who was a very fine player, he never played that way.
No.
He was always -- doodle-de, doodle-de, doodle-de -- you know?
Yeah.
But you always, like, all over the place, and then you come on back in.
Yeah.
And did that -- but if you listen to your early recordings, like --
Well, see, that's the way my mind was going.
Yeah. It was moving in that direction.
Yeah. All through them notes that was being hit.
Uh-huh.
I mean, my mind always told me something to put in it.
Right.
To make it come out right. And I'd catch that beat at the end.
